content.audio:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Greenhill Summer English Course. My name is Grace Mwangi, and I'm the course manager. I'd like to tell you a few important things about the next two weeks.
First, classes. Lessons start every day at nine o'clock and finish at half past twelve. There is a short break at half past ten, and you can get free tea and coffee in the student cafe on the ground floor. Please be on time. If you are more than fifteen minutes late, you must wait until the break before you go into the classroom.
In the afternoons, we have activities. On Mondays and Wednesdays there is a sports afternoon in the park behind the school. On Tuesdays we visit a museum or a gallery in the city. On Thursdays you can join our cooking club. Last year the students made dishes from twelve different countries, and it was everyone's favourite activity. Fridays are free, so you can rest or go shopping.
At the weekend, there is a trip to the seaside on Saturday. The bus leaves from the front of the school at eight o'clock in the morning. The trip costs fifteen pounds, and you need to pay at reception before Thursday. On Sunday there are no activities.
Now, a few rules. Please don't use your phone in class, unless your teacher asks you to. And please speak English as much as you can, also with your friends at lunch. It's the best way to learn quickly.
Finally, if you have any problems, with your room, your classes or anything else, come and see me in my office. It's on the first floor, room twelve, and I'm there from eight until five every day. Right, now let's find your classrooms. Students in group A, please follow Lucas. Group B, please come with me.

A: Today on Community Voices I'm talking to Ana Ferreira, who started a repair cafe in our town two years ago. Ana, what exactly is a repair cafe?
B: Well, it's a free event where people bring things that are broken, like lamps, bikes, clothes or small kitchen machines, and volunteers help them fix them. We meet on the first Saturday of every month in the library hall.
A: Why did you decide to start it?
B: It started with my toaster, actually. It stopped working, and the shop told me it was cheaper to buy a new one than to repair it. That made me angry, because the problem was just one small part. I thought, there must be lots of people who feel the same.
A: And were you right?
B: Completely. At the first event we expected about twenty people, and nearly eighty came. We didn't have enough volunteers, so some people had to come back the next month.
A: Who are the volunteers?
B: All kinds of people. Retired engineers, students, and a tailor called Mr Adeyemi, who is brilliant with clothes. Some of our best volunteers are teenagers who are good with phones and computers.
A: Some people say that repairing things is old-fashioned. What do you think?
B: I don't agree at all. Fixing things saves money, and it means less rubbish. But for me, the most important thing is that people learn. We don't just repair the item for you. You sit next to the volunteer and do it together, so next time you can do it yourself.
A: Do you ever fail?
B: Of course. About one in four things can't be repaired. But even then, people usually leave happy, because they understand what the problem was.
A: What are your plans for the future?
B: We'd like to open a second repair cafe in the next town. We're looking for a room there, and we always need more volunteers, especially people who can fix bikes. That's our biggest need at the moment.
A: Ana Ferreira, thank you very much.

content.passage:
My first month in Melbourne
by Sofia Lindqvist

Four weeks ago I moved from Stockholm to Melbourne in Australia. I am a primary school teacher, and I got a job at a small school near the city centre. I want to write about my first month here, because many of my friends at home have asked me about it.

The first week was not easy. The flight was very long, more than twenty-four hours, and I was tired for days. I stayed in a hotel because my flat was not ready yet. Everything felt different: the food, the weather and even the way people speak English. I studied English at school for many years, but at first I didn't understand some of the words that people here use every day.

In the second week, I moved into my flat. It is small, but it has a balcony, and I can see a park from my window. My neighbour, an older woman called Mrs Tran, came to say hello on my first evening. She brought me some soup and told me about the best shops in the area. Since then, we often have tea together on Sundays.

Starting work was exciting but also a bit scary. My class has twenty-six children, aged seven and eight. They were very interested in Sweden, and they asked me lots of questions. Is it dark all the time? Do you have kangaroos? (No, we don't!) The other teachers have been very kind and helpful. One of them, Mr Mensah, showed me how everything works at the school.

The thing I like most about Melbourne is that there is always something to do. There are markets, free concerts and lovely beaches not far from the city. The thing I like least is the weather. People say that Melbourne can have four seasons in one day, and it's true. In the morning it is sunny and warm, and in the afternoon it is cold and windy. I always carry a jacket now!

Do I miss home? Yes, sometimes. I miss my family, and I miss Swedish bread. But I talk to my parents every weekend on video, and I am making new friends here. If you are thinking about moving to another country, my advice is simple: be patient. The first weeks are hard, but it gets better.

content.passage:
The library where you can borrow a tent

In most libraries, you can borrow books, films and perhaps a laptop. But at the public library in Ridgeford, a small town of about 40,000 people, you can also borrow a tent, a sewing machine, a guitar or even a telescope. The 'Library of Things' opened there eighteen months ago, and it has become one of the most popular services in the town.

The idea came from Meera Pillai, who has worked at the library for eleven years. 'I noticed that people often bought expensive things that they only used once or twice,' she explains. 'My neighbour bought a drill to put up one shelf, and then it stayed in a cupboard for five years. I thought, why can't we share these things, like we share books?'

At first, not everyone liked the idea. Some members of the town council worried that items would be broken or never returned. 'They were right to ask questions,' says Meera. 'So we started small, with just forty items, and we made clear rules.' Members can borrow up to two things at a time, for one week. There is no charge, but if you return something late, you pay a small fee, and if you break something, you must pay for the repair.

The results have surprised even Meera. Today the library has more than three hundred items, and most of them were given by local people. Only a few things have been lost, and there have been very few problems with damage. The most popular items are the carpet cleaner, the camping equipment and, surprisingly, the ice-cream machine, which is booked almost every weekend in summer.

Users are enthusiastic. Tomasz Kowalski, a father of two, borrowed a tent before buying one. 'We wanted to find out if our children actually enjoyed camping,' he says. 'They loved it, so we bought our own. But if they had hated it, we would have saved a lot of money.' Student Grace Adebayo says the service has helped her to try new hobbies. 'I've borrowed a sewing machine and a keyboard. I could never afford to buy them both.'

Not everyone is a fan, though. A local shop owner, who did not want to give his name, said the library was taking business away from shops in the town. Meera disagrees. 'Many people try something here and then go and buy their own, like Tomasz did. I think we help the shops more than we hurt them.'

Other towns are now interested. Meera has already given advice to libraries in three nearby towns, and she hopes that one day every library will have a collection of things as well as books. 'Libraries have always been about sharing,' she says. 'This is just a new way of doing it.'
